    Persistent sessions

    sessions.Rmd

    atlas() is a one-call wrapper around an AtlasSession — an R6 object that holds the conversation, the R environment the agent works in, and a run directory on disk. The session outlives the call: use it for follow-ups, and resume it after a crash or restart.

    The session object 

    library(Atlas)

s <- AtlasSession$new(mtcars, outcome = "mpg", n_models = 3,
                      goal = "prioritise interpretability")
res <- s$build()                 # the full agentic loop
s$tell("swap model 2 for a GAM") # follow-up in the same context
s$check()                        # re-verify constraints right now
s$results()                      # assemble a fresh results object

    res$session from atlas() is the same thing — every result carries its live session, so res$session$tell("why did model 1 win?") continues the conversation with full memory of the build.

    Iterative follow-ups inherit the session’s stopping rules (patience attempts without improvement; improvements under the min_improve fraction don’t count), so “keep refining the features until it stops improving” terminates on its own:

    s <- AtlasSession$new(mtcars, "mpg", n_models = 3,   # n_models is a maximum
                      patience = 3, min_improve = 0.05)  # 0.05 = 5%
res <- s$build()
s$tell("take the best model and refine its feature engineering until
        performance stops improving")

    What’s on disk

    Each session owns a run directory (default .atlas/<timestamp>, or pass dir =):

    file contents
    data.rds the training data, so a resume works cold
    meta.rds outcome, n_models, goal, constraints
    code.R every code chunk the agent ran, human-readable
    code.rds the same chunks, exactly as recorded (for replay)
    turns.rds the full conversation
    report.md the agent’s final report
    leaderboard.csv validation metrics per model
    models.rds the fitted models

    Checkpoints are written after every tool call and every reply, so at most the in-flight step is lost to a crash. code.R doubles as the reproducibility artifact: it is plain R you can read, audit, or run without Atlas.

    Resuming 

    s <- atlas_resume(".atlas/20260703-141500")
s$tell("continue where you left off")

    Resume does not try to deserialize the working environment. It reloads the data, replays the recorded code log top to bottom (agent code is seeded, so this is exact), and restores the conversation turns — the agent comes back knowing everything it did, with all fitted objects rebuilt. The one thing to budget for: replay refits the models, so resuming a session whose models take minutes to fit takes those minutes again.

    Interrupting a running build

    You don’t have to wait for the agent to ask. In the console, interrupt with Ctrl+C / Esc, then resume with the new information — because every code chunk is checkpointed as it runs, the agent’s work up to the interruption is preserved and replayed:

    res <- atlas(big_data, "claim_cost")   # Ctrl+C mid-build...
s <- atlas_resume(".atlas/20260703-141500")
s$tell("stop trying tree models; the deployment target only supports GLMs")

    For programmatic front-ends, the underlying hook is the interject constructor argument: a function() polled after every tool call. Return a message to interrupt the agent (it is delivered with its next tool result, marked as the highest-priority instruction), or NULL when there is nothing to say.

    Human-in-the-loop

    The agent has an ask_user tool. In an interactive R session it prints the question under an ── atlas needs your input ── rule and blocks on the console — that’s how plan approval works. In non-interactive contexts (Rscript, CI) the tool tells the agent to use its best judgment and record the decision in the final report, so scripted runs never hang.

    Verbosity

    verbose = TRUE (default) streams the agent’s narration, each code chunk under an ── R ── rule, its output as #> lines, and constraint-check tables. verbose = FALSE runs silently; everything is still checkpointed to the run directory, so report.md and code.R tell the story afterwards.
